title: Here's a Ligand, Go Design a Protein
body_text: When I get asked what areas of drug design are the most amenable to being changed by AI/ML techniques, my general answer is “proteins and antibodies”. That takes no great imaginative leap on my part, because the current protein structure prediction (and protein design) tools are often (although not invariably!) quite impressive - and particularly so compared to the state of the art in small molecules. Antibodies are probably the shortest path to making actual drugs with these tools as well, since there are already numerous extremely useful examples on the market, due to their intrinsic biological advantages as a class. These include long plasma half lives, the possibility of extraordinary selectivity (or perhaps extraordinary bi-specificity if you want to get fancy), and more. This new paper only adds to that conviction of mine. The authors are attacking a particularly hard problem: how do you come up with a de novo protein that will bind a particular small molecule? That’s a longer step to delivering actual drugs, because we’re not often in the position to need such a protein therapeutically, but the science behind it speaks to the generally very important problem of how proteins bind small molecules at all. We drug discovery types would be even more interested in the setup of “Given this here protein, tell me about some new small molecule scaffolds that will bind tightly to it”, but the focus of this paper (“Given this here small molecule, tell me about some new proteins that will bind to it”) cannot help but be informative as well. The authors do this by using what they call a “ligand-aware sequence engineering message-passing neural network” and combining that with a structure predictor module that tries to model a protein-ligand complex for a given protein sequence/small molecule combination. The former is trained on ligand-bound structures from the PDB, which is definitely the place to start (even though it may still not be large enough a data set to guarantee success). Sending queries around these two processes in a closed loop seems to do a pretty impressive job of producing new binding proteins, and the overall workflow is given the name “neural iterative selection-expansion” (NISE). The authors note that this is essentially a self-consistency optimization process, and that the coupling of protein sequence/backbone refinement and ligand conformation is likely to be more efficient than trying to take these one at a time. They tried this idea out on two small molecule test cases, the camptothecin analog exatecan and the anticoagulant apixapan. These seem to be as good a choice as any. Exatecan targets the enzyme topoisomerase, and more specifically topoisomerase/DNA complexes, and doesn’t seem to have any odd or strong plasma protein binding behavior on its own. It’s a popular “warhead” in antibody-drug conjugate design. Apixaban’s protein target is Factor Xa, and it has pretty normal-sounding plasma protein binding otherwise (87%). The team used a couple of binding examples (biotin/avidin and PiB/rucaparib) with these held out from the training set, and the results were encouraging. For exatecan, the team was looking for a protein that would bind to the drug and protect its lactone ring from hydrolysis - the opened form is much less cell-penetrating and (unlike the parent compound) strongly binds serum albumin. You could imagine such a protector protein as part of a delivery vehicle for the drug, although the feasibility of that idea is in the end a separate issue from just getting the binding part to work from scratch at all. There are no exatecan-containing protein structures in the PDB itself, although there are a few (for example) with camptothecin and other related compounds. Using their technique to generate a four-helix-bundle protein (a class that has been shown in the past to be amenable to small-molecule binding design) gave four candidates, all of which bound the compound. The best of them had a Kd of 0.12 micromolar, which was a considerable improvement over the candidates generated by a more conventional workflow. You can see the crystal structure of that complex here. That best protein was also selective for exatecan over camptothecin and other compounds in this class by at least 50-fold. And sending this sequence back around through the system for single-amino-acid substitution ideas returned proteins that showed single-digit-nanomolar affinity. All of these also seem to do a very good job of preserving the lactone from from hydrolysis, so this has to be considered a success. For apixaban the team chose a different protein scaffold, an NTF2 backbone that has also been shown to bind various small molecules (including apixaban, using Rosetta). The best of those got down to a 680 nM Kd. A strong apixaban binder could conceivably be used as an inactivating antidote, which is always a consideration with anticoagulants. The optimization process yielded six candidate proteins, five of which successfully bound the drug, with the best showing an impressive Kd of 80 picomolar (!), which is as strong as it binds to Factor Xa. So overall this looks like a promising technique, although it’s more computationally intensive than my brief overview here has probably made it seem. It will be interesting to see this applied to a broader selection of small molecules (and a broader selection of potential binding scaffolds), and the authors seem interesting in trying just these sorts of experiments. They say that “We expect NISE to work with any (protein) fold that can be modeled accurately by co-structure predictors”, and we need to find out what that statement encompasses.
